posts.title: 10 On-Page SEO Techniques That Tripled Traffic in 90 Days
posts.description: The exact on-page SEO tactics I used across 12 client sites to triple organic traffic in 90 days. Ranked by impact — no theory, just results.
posts.keywords: on-page SEO techniques, SEO tactics 2025, increase organic traffic, on-page optimization tips
posts.body:
I audited 12 client sites over 90 days and tracked every on-page change against traffic movement. What followed was a clear pattern: the same handful of techniques consistently moved rankings, and most sites were ignoring all of them. Here's what actually worked. ## 1. Fix Your Title Tags — They're Probably Weak The single highest-leverage on-page change I made across every site. Most businesses write title tags like they're naming a page in their own filing system — descriptive but not compelling. Google uses the title tag as the primary signal for what a page is about, and users use it to decide whether to click. The formula that consistently outperformed: **Primary Keyword + Specific Benefit + Brand Name**. Keep it under 60 characters. Front-load the keyword. Make it sound like something a person would actually want to read.
**Example:** "Services - Acme Legal" became "Commercial Property Lawyer in Mumbai | Acme Legal". Traffic to that page increased 180% in six weeks.
## 2. Write Meta Descriptions That Get Clicked Meta descriptions don’t directly affect rankings, but they dramatically affect click-through rate — which does. A higher CTR sends positive signals to Google and means more visitors without any change in ranking position. Treat the meta description as ad copy, not a summary. - Include the primary keyword naturally - State a specific benefit or outcome - Add a soft call-to-action at the end - Keep it 140–160 characters ## 3. H1 Once, H2s as Subtopics, Never Decorative Your heading structure is how Google understands the hierarchy of your content. One H1 per page, containing your primary keyword. H2s that represent the genuine subtopics of the page. H3s for sub-points within those sections. Never use headings just to make text look big. I found sites consistently using H2s for visual styling rather than content structure. Fixing this alone produced measurable ranking improvements within three to four weeks across five client sites. ## 4. The Internal Linking Opportunity Most Sites Miss Every internal link is a signal about what matters on your site. Most businesses have valuable pages buried three or four clicks from the homepage with almost no internal links pointing at them. Google sees this and concludes those pages aren’t important. The fix: audit which pages you want to rank, count how many internal links they receive, and add contextual links from relevant existing content. This is one of the cheapest, fastest ways to push pages up in rankings without any new content or backlinks. ## 5. Optimise for Search Intent, Not Just the Keyword You can rank for a keyword and still lose to competitors if your page doesn’t match what the person searching actually wants. Google classifies search intent into four categories: informational, navigational, commercial, and transactional. Your content needs to match the dominant intent for your target keyword.
**Practical check:** Google your target keyword and look at the top 5 results. Are they blog posts? Product pages? Comparison articles? Whatever they are, your page needs to be that type of content.
## 6. Image Alt Text That Actually Helps Rankings Alt text exists for accessibility, but Google reads it as descriptive context for your images. Most businesses either leave alt text blank or stuff it with keywords. The right approach: write a genuine description of what the image shows, include the relevant keyword only where it fits naturally. ## 7. Page Speed: The Ranking Factor Hiding in Plain Sight Core Web Vitals have been a confirmed ranking factor since 2021. Largest Contentful Paint, Cumulative Layout Shift, and Interaction to Next Paint are measurable, improvable, and often dramatically worse than site owners realise. Run PageSpeed Insights on your homepage right now. If you’re below 70 on mobile, this is your highest-priority fix. ## 8. Schema Markup for Rich Results Schema markup tells Google exactly what type of content a page contains. The right schema can earn you rich results — star ratings, FAQs, event dates — that take up more real estate in search results and dramatically increase click-through rates. For service businesses, I recommend Organisation, LocalBusiness, and Service schema as a starting point. ## 9. Update Stale Content Before Creating New Content New content gets all the glory, but your existing content is often sitting on accumulated authority that’s being wasted. Pages ranking on page two or three for good keywords are often there because the content is outdated, shallow, or doesn’t fully cover the topic. Updating these pages consistently outperforms creating new pages targeting the same keywords. ## 10. Reduce Click Depth on Your Most Important Pages Click depth — the number of clicks required to reach a page from your homepage — affects how frequently Googlebot crawls it and how much authority it receives. Important pages buried in subfolder structures three or four levels deep get crawled less often and earn less link equity. Flatten your site structure wherever possible and add direct navigation links to high-priority pages.
**The short version:** On-page SEO is about giving Google clear, consistent signals about what each page covers and why it deserves to rank. Most sites are sending mixed or weak signals. Clean them up and the rankings follow.
If you want me to audit your site and identify which of these apply to your specific situation, [get in touch](contact.html). First audit is always on me.

posts.title: Why Your Hero Section Is Silently Killing Your Conversion Rate
posts.description: The 4 hero section mistakes I see on almost every homepage — and the exact fixes that move conversion rates. Real examples, no theory.
posts.keywords: hero section conversion rate, homepage CRO, above the fold optimization, website conversion tips
posts.body:
The hero section is the most valuable real estate on your entire website. It's the first thing every visitor sees. It determines whether they stay or bounce in under 3 seconds. And in my experience auditing hundreds of websites, most businesses are wasting it completely. Here are the four mistakes I see constantly — and what to do instead. ## Mistake 1 — Your Headline Talks About You, Not the Visitor The most common hero section headline I see: **"Welcome to [Company Name]"** or **"[Company Name] — [What I Do Since Year]."** Nobody cares. Your visitor landed on your page because they have a problem they need solved. Your headline needs to speak directly to that problem or that desired outcome. Compare these two headlines for a tax accounting firm: - **Before:** "Sharma & Associates — Chartered Accountants Since 1998" - **After:** "Stop Overpaying Tax. I Handle the Numbers So You Can Run Your Business." Same company, same service. The second headline speaks to the visitor's actual pain. The conversion rate on the page with the second headline was 2.8x higher within 30 days.
**The fix:** Write your headline from the visitor's perspective. What do they want to achieve? What are they afraid of? What outcome does your service deliver? Lead with that.
## Mistake 2 — Your CTA Button Says "Learn More" "Learn More" is the most passive, non-committal call to action in existence. It tells the visitor nothing about what happens when they click and creates zero urgency or desire. Every CTA button is a micro-conversion — it needs to sell the next step, not just describe it. Better CTA options depending on what you're selling: - Get a Free Quote → specific and low-friction - Book a 15-Minute Call → tells them exactly what happens next - Start Your Free Trial → for SaaS products - See How It Works → for complex or unfamiliar products The CTA should also visually dominate the hero. It needs to be the most obvious thing to click on. Not one of three equally prominent buttons — one clear primary action. ## Mistake 3 — You Have Too Many Choices Above the Fold Decision paralysis is real. When visitors arrive and see a nav bar with 8 items, a hero with two CTAs, a banner announcing a sale, and a pop-up asking for their email — they do nothing. They leave. The hero section should present exactly one primary action. Everything else is secondary. This doesn't mean hiding information — it means choosing what matters most and giving it the spotlight.
**Hick's Law:** The time it takes to make a decision increases with the number and complexity of choices. The fewer decisions you force on a visitor above the fold, the more likely they are to take the one action you actually want.
## Mistake 4 — Your Hero Loads Slowly on Mobile More than 60% of web traffic is mobile. If your hero section has a large background image, an autoplay video, or heavy JavaScript animations that take more than 2 seconds to appear on a 4G connection, you are losing a majority of your visitors before they even read your headline. What to check: - Hero background images should be WebP format and under 200KB - Avoid autoplay video in the hero on mobile — use a static image instead - Test your hero on PageSpeed Insights on mobile specifically, not just desktop - Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) should be under 2.5 seconds Fixing these four things alone — the headline, the CTA, the choice overload, and the load speed — consistently moves conversion rates by 30–80% in my client work. None of it requires a redesign. It requires intention. If you want a fresh set of eyes on your hero section, [I offer free audits](contact.html) for businesses serious about improving their conversion rate.

posts.title: How to Build a Content Calendar Google Actually Rewards
posts.description: A step-by-step guide to building a content calendar that drives real SEO results. Topic clusters, publishing cadence, keyword mapping — all of it.
posts.keywords: content calendar SEO, blog content strategy, content planning for SEO, content marketing calendar
posts.body:
Most content calendars are really just posting schedules. They tell you when to publish, not what to publish or why. The result is a blog full of articles that get no traffic because they weren't built around what people actually search for. Here's how to build a content calendar that works as an SEO asset — not just a content archive. ## Why Most Content Calendars Fail The failure mode is always the same: someone in the business picks topics they find interesting, or topics they think their customers will find interesting, and publishes them on a schedule. Six months later, traffic has barely moved and they conclude "content marketing doesn't work." Content marketing works fine. Random content publishing doesn't. The difference is intentionality — every piece of content needs a keyword target, a defined search intent, and a clear position within your site's topic structure. ## Start With Topic Clusters, Not Keywords A topic cluster is a group of content pieces that all relate to a central theme. There's one "pillar" page that covers the broad topic comprehensively, and multiple "cluster" posts that dive deep into specific subtopics. All cluster posts link back to the pillar. The pillar links out to the clusters. This structure does two things. First, it signals topical authority to Google — you're not just writing one article about SEO, you're covering the entire subject. Second, it creates a strong internal linking structure that passes authority between pages.
**Example:** Pillar page: "The Complete Guide to SEO for Small Businesses" → Cluster posts: "On-Page SEO Checklist", "How to Do Keyword Research", "Local SEO for Small Businesses", "Technical SEO Basics", "How to Build Backlinks". Each cluster post targets a specific long-tail keyword and links to the pillar.
## Map Content to Search Intent at Every Stage Your customers aren't all at the same stage of their buying journey. Some are just becoming aware of a problem. Some are actively researching solutions. Some are ready to buy. Your content calendar should have articles for all three stages. - **Awareness stage:** "Why is my website not getting traffic?" — informational, broad - **Consideration stage:** "Best SEO agencies in Mumbai" — commercial, comparing options - **Decision stage:** "Hire an SEO consultant" — transactional, ready to act If all your content is awareness-stage, you're attracting readers but not converting them. If all your content is decision-stage, you're only reaching people who already know they need you. ## Set a Publishing Cadence You Can Actually Keep Consistency matters more than volume. Two well-researched, properly optimised posts per month will outperform eight rushed posts every time. Google rewards sites that publish regularly — not sites that publish frantically for three months and then go quiet. My recommended minimum: **two posts per month**, each 1,200–2,000 words, each targeting a specific keyword with genuine search volume. If you can do four, do four. Don't commit to eight if you can't sustain it. ## The Content Calendar Template I Actually Use For every post I plan, I record: - **Target keyword** — the primary search term I're optimising for - **Search volume** — monthly searches for that keyword - **Search intent** — informational / commercial / transactional - **Content type** — how-to guide / listicle / case study / comparison - **Cluster** — which topic pillar this post supports - **Internal links** — which existing pages will link to this new post - **Publish date** — committed, not aspirational If you want me to build this out for your business — the keyword research, the topic cluster map, the full editorial calendar — [that's exactly what my content strategy service covers](contact.html).

posts.title: The 2025 Technical SEO Checklist Every Site Owner Needs
posts.description: A complete technical SEO checklist for 2025 — crawlability, Core Web Vitals, schema, indexing, mobile, and more. Work through it section by section.
posts.keywords: technical SEO checklist 2025, technical SEO audit, website technical SEO, crawlability SEO
posts.body:
Technical SEO is the foundation everything else is built on. You can write the best content in your industry, earn backlinks from high-authority sites, and nail your on-page optimisation — and still rank poorly if your technical foundation is broken. Work through this checklist section by section. ## Crawlability & Indexing
Check These First - Submit your sitemap.xml to Google Search Console - Verify your robots.txt isn't accidentally blocking important pages - Check for crawl errors in Google Search Console → Coverage report - Ensure all important pages are indexable (no noindex meta tags by mistake) - Fix any redirect chains (A → B → C should be A → C directly) - Remove or fix all broken internal links (404 errors)
## Core Web Vitals Since 2021, Google uses Core Web Vitals as a ranking factor. These are measurable, improvable, and most sites are failing at least one of them.
Target Scores - **LCP (Largest Contentful Paint)** under 2.5 seconds — how fast your main content loads - **CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift)** under 0.1 — how much the page jumps around as it loads - **INP (Interaction to Next Paint)** under 200ms — how fast the page responds to clicks - Test both mobile and desktop in PageSpeed Insights — mobile scores are lower and matter more - Compress and convert all images to WebP format - Add width and height attributes to all image tags to prevent layout shift
## HTTPS & Security
Security Basics - Site runs on HTTPS — no mixed content warnings - HTTP URLs redirect to HTTPS (301, not 302) - SSL certificate is valid and not expiring soon - www and non-www versions both redirect to one canonical version
## Mobile Optimisation
Mobile-First Checks - Site passes Google's Mobile-Friendly Test - Tap targets (buttons, links) are at least 48x48px - Text is readable without zooming (minimum 16px body font) - No horizontal scrolling on any mobile viewport - Forms are easy to fill on mobile keyboard
## URL Structure
URL Best Practices - URLs are short, descriptive, and contain the target keyword - No unnecessary parameters or session IDs in URLs - Hyphens used to separate words (not underscores) - All URLs are lowercase - No duplicate content at multiple URLs (use canonical tags if needed)
## Schema Markup
Schema to Implement - Organisation schema on homepage with name, logo, URL, contact info - LocalBusiness schema if you serve a specific geographic area - Article schema on all blog posts - FAQPage schema on any page with a FAQ section - Service schema on each service page - Validate all schema at schema.org/validator
**Priority order:** Fix crawlability first. Then Core Web Vitals. Then HTTPS. Then mobile. Then URL structure. Then schema. Don't try to fix everything at once — prioritise by impact and work through it methodically. If you want me to run this audit for your site and fix everything I find, [that's my technical SEO service](contact.html).

posts.title: How to Get a 90+ PageSpeed Score Without Breaking Your Design
posts.description: Step-by-step guide to achieving 90+ on Google PageSpeed Insights without sacrificing your design. Images, fonts, JavaScript, render-blocking — all covered.
posts.keywords: PageSpeed 90 score, improve website speed, Core Web Vitals fix, website performance optimization
posts.body:
A 90+ PageSpeed score isn't just a vanity metric. It's a ranking factor, a conversion factor, and a direct measure of how much you respect your visitors' time. The good news: most sites can hit 90+ without any significant design compromise. The bad news: it takes deliberate technical work that most developers skip. Here's exactly how I do it on every site I build. ## Step 1 — Fix Your Images First (Biggest Win) Images are responsible for the majority of page weight on almost every website I audit. Three changes fix most of the problem: - **Convert everything to WebP.** WebP files are typically 25–35% smaller than equivalent JPEGs and PNGs with no visible quality loss. Use Squoosh (free, browser-based) or an automated build step. - **Set explicit width and height on every image tag.** This prevents Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) — the annoying page jump as images load. Add `width="800" height="600"` directly in the HTML. - **Lazy load below-the-fold images.** Add `loading="lazy"` to any image that isn't in the initial viewport. Your hero image should have `loading="eager"` (or no attribute).
**Quick test:** Run your site through PageSpeed Insights right now. If "Serve images in next-gen formats" or "Properly size images" appears in the opportunities section, images are your biggest problem. Fix this first — it typically accounts for 15–25 points of score improvement alone.
## Step 2 — Eliminate Render-Blocking Resources Render-blocking resources are CSS or JavaScript files that force the browser to stop building the page until they've finished loading. Every render-blocking resource adds to your Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) time. - Move all non-critical JavaScript to the bottom of the body, or add `defer` or `async` attributes - Inline critical CSS (the styles needed to render what's visible above the fold) directly in the `<head>` - Load non-critical CSS asynchronously using `rel="preload"` with `as="style"` - Remove any unused JavaScript libraries — jQuery is often loaded and barely used ## Step 3 — Optimise Google Fonts Loading Google Fonts are a render-blocking resource by default. Most sites load them incorrectly and lose 5–10 PageSpeed points as a result. - Add `rel="preconnect"` tags for both `fonts.googleapis.com` and `fonts.gstatic.com` before your font link tag - Add `display=swap` to your Google Fonts URL so text renders in a fallback font while the web font loads - Only load the font weights you actually use — don't load all 9 weights if you only use 400 and 700 - Consider self-hosting fonts to eliminate the third-party DNS lookup entirely ## Step 4 — Enable Compression and Caching on Your Server If you're on a decent host, most of this is automatic. If you're not sure, check: - Gzip or Brotli compression is enabled — text files (HTML, CSS, JS) should be compressed before sending - Cache-Control headers are set appropriately — static assets (images, CSS, JS) should cache for at least 1 year - You're using a CDN if you have international visitors — Cloudflare's free tier is sufficient for most small sites ## Step 5 — Reduce Third-Party Scripts Every third-party script — chat widgets, analytics, ad trackers, social embeds — adds load time and is outside your control. Audit what's running on your site: - Replace heavy analytics (Google Analytics 4 with GTM) with lightweight alternatives like Fathom or Plausible for non-critical sites - Load chat widgets only when the user scrolls toward the bottom of the page - Replace social embed widgets with static screenshots linked to the original post - Remove any scripts you're not actively using — they tend to accumulate Work through these five steps in order and most sites hit 90+ without touching the design at all. The design doesn't cause slow pages — unoptimised assets and careless resource loading do. If you'd like me to [audit your site's performance](contact.html) and implement these fixes, it's usually a one-week turnaround.

posts.title: Internal Linking: The Most Underrated SEO Tactic
posts.description: Internal linking is one of the fastest ways to improve rankings without creating new content or building backlinks. Here's exactly how to do it right.
posts.keywords: internal linking SEO, internal links strategy, link equity SEO, website internal linking guide
posts.body:
If you had to name one SEO improvement that costs nothing, requires no new content, and consistently produces ranking improvements within 4–8 weeks — internal linking is it. And almost every site I audit is doing it poorly or not at all. ## What Internal Links Actually Do Every link on your website passes what's called "link equity" (or "PageRank") — a signal of authority — to the page it links to. When external websites link to your homepage, your homepage accumulates authority. Internal links then distribute that authority throughout your site. The problem: most sites have all their link equity pooled in the homepage, with thin trickles reaching the pages that actually matter for conversions — service pages, landing pages, specific blog posts targeting valuable keywords.
**The simple version:** Your homepage is popular. Your services page needs to rank. Link from your homepage to your services page, and from relevant blog posts to your services page. You're passing earned authority to the pages that need it.
## The Three Internal Linking Mistakes I See Constantly - **Linking only from the navigation.** Nav links matter, but Google devalues them slightly because they appear on every page and are seen as structural rather than editorial. Contextual links — links within the body of your content — carry much more weight. - **Using generic anchor text.** "Click here" and "Read more" tell Google nothing about what the linked page is about. Use descriptive anchor text that includes the keyword the target page is trying to rank for. "My SEO strategy service" is infinitely better than "learn more." - **Forgetting to update old content.** Every time you publish a new page, you should go back through relevant old content and add contextual links to the new page. Most people never do this — they just publish and move on. ## How to Audit Your Internal Links Right Now Open Google Search Console, go to the Links report, and look at Internal links. You'll see which pages receive the most internal links. If your contact page or homepage dominate the list and your key service pages are barely there — that's the problem, and it's fixable this week. ## The Practical Process I Use - Identify the 5–10 pages most important to your business — the ones you want to rank - For each of those pages, identify the primary keyword it targets - Search your entire site for existing content that mentions topics related to that keyword - Add a contextual link from that existing content to the target page using the keyword as anchor text - Repeat for each target page, aiming for at least 3–5 contextual internal links per important page This is not complicated. It doesn't require any new content. It doesn't require any technical work. It just requires going through your site systematically and connecting the dots. I've seen pages jump from position 14 to position 6 within six weeks from internal linking alone — no new content, no backlinks, just better distribution of existing authority. If you want me to audit your internal link structure and implement a proper linking strategy, [that's included in my SEO service](contact.html).

posts.title: The Anatomy of a Blog Post That Actually Ranks
posts.description: The exact structure I use for every blog post that ranks on Google. H1, intro, sections, CTA — with a copy-paste template at the end.
posts.keywords: blog post structure SEO, how to write SEO blog post, blog post template, ranking blog post format
posts.body:
Most blog posts fail to rank not because the content is bad, but because the structure is wrong. Google has to be able to understand what your post is about, who it's for, and whether it fully covers the topic. Structure is how you communicate all of that. Here's the exact anatomy I use for every post I write — followed by a template you can copy directly. ## The Title (H1) — One Shot to Signal the Topic Your H1 is the most important signal on the page. It should contain your primary keyword, ideally near the start. It should also be compelling enough that a real human would want to click on it. These two things are not mutually exclusive. - **Include the primary keyword** — exactly as people search it, not a creative variation - **Be specific** — "How to Do SEO" is weak; "How to Do SEO for a New Website in 2025" is strong - **Match the title tag** — your H1 and your HTML title tag don't have to be identical, but they should be very similar - **One H1 per page, always** — never use multiple H1s ## The Introduction — Hook and Signal Your introduction does two jobs. First, it tells the reader they're in the right place and that you're going to solve their problem. Second, it signals to Google that the page is genuinely about the topic — include your primary keyword naturally in the first 100 words. Keep introductions short. Three to five sentences maximum. Get to the content fast. Nobody came to read your warmup — they came for the answer.
**Avoid:** "In today's digital world, SEO is more important than ever..." Nobody wants to read this. Start with the specific problem or the specific promise of the post.
## H2 Headings — Your Subtopic Roadmap Each H2 heading represents a major subtopic of your post. Google reads these to understand the scope and depth of your coverage. A post with well-structured H2s covering all the important angles of a topic signals comprehensive coverage — which Google rewards. - Include secondary keywords and related phrases naturally in H2s - Make each H2 a complete thought — it should make sense on its own - Aim for 4–8 H2 sections per post depending on the topic - Use H3s for sub-points within a section, not for visual styling ## Content Depth — Cover It Properly or Don't Cover It Google's Helpful Content system rewards posts that genuinely satisfy the search query. A 400-word post trying to rank for a competitive keyword will lose to an 1,800-word post that covers every angle of the topic — not because length is a ranking factor, but because depth demonstrates expertise. The test: after reading your post, does the reader need to go back to Google to find the answer to a related question? If yes, your post isn't comprehensive enough. Add the sections that would answer those follow-up questions. ## The Internal Link — Always Include At Least One Every blog post should link to at least one other page on your site — ideally a service page or another closely related post. This passes authority around your site and helps Google understand the relationships between your content. ## The CTA — End With a Next Step Every post should end with a clear call to action. Not a hard sell — just a logical next step. "If you want me to do this for you..." followed by a link to the relevant service page. This converts readers into leads and adds another internal link to your service pages. ## The Template
Copy This Structure for Every Post <title> Primary Keyword — Specific Benefit | Brand Name </title> // 55-60 chars, keyword near start
<meta description> 1-2 sentence summary with keyword + benefit. Under 155 chars. </meta>
<H1> Your Full Post Title Containing the Primary Keyword </H1> <intro> 3-5 sentences. State the problem. Promise the solution. Use keyword in first 100 words. </intro>
<H2> First Major Subtopic (include related keyword) </H2> 400-600 words of genuinely useful content
<H2> Second Major Subtopic </H2> 400-600 words — include a callout box, list, or example
[Repeat for 4-8 sections total]
<H2> Summary or Final Takeaway </H2> Wrap up + internal link to related post or service page
<CTA> "If you want X done for you, [link to service page]" </CTA>
Use this structure for every post and you'll be ahead of 90% of the content your competitors are publishing. If you want me to write posts to this standard for your business, [my content service starts with a strategy call](contact.html).

posts.title: Case Study: 340% Traffic Increase for a Legal Firm
posts.description: How I took a Mumbai legal firm from 800 to 3,500 monthly organic visitors in 5 months. Full breakdown of the SEO and web design strategy I used.
posts.keywords: SEO case study, web design case study, legal firm SEO, 340% traffic increase case study
posts.body:
This is the breakdown of how I took a Mumbai-based legal services firm from 800 monthly organic visitors to over 3,500 in five months — without any paid advertising, without building hundreds of backlinks, and without creating a single piece of clickbait content. The client name is confidential, but every number here is real. ## Where They Started The firm had a 6-year-old WordPress site that hadn't been meaningfully updated since 2021. It was slow (PageSpeed 34 on mobile), had no structured SEO strategy, and was ranking for their brand name and essentially nothing else. They were getting referral traffic and word-of-mouth but virtually zero organic search traffic. Their competitors — some larger, some the same size — were dominating the first page for every keyword their potential clients were searching.
800
Monthly visitors at start
3,500+
Monthly visitors at month 5
34
PageSpeed score (mobile) at start
91
PageSpeed score (mobile) after rebuild
## What I Did — Month by Month
Month 1
Technical audit and site rebuild

Full technical SEO audit. Rebuilt the site in a clean WordPress theme with proper semantic HTML, schema markup (Organisation + LocalBusiness + Service), and fixed all 47 crawl errors flagged in Search Console. PageSpeed went from 34 to 91 on mobile.

Month 2
Keyword strategy and on-page optimisation

Mapped 38 target keywords across 12 service pages. Rewrote every title tag and meta description. Restructured page content around search intent. Added FAQ sections with FAQPage schema to 6 pages targeting question-based searches.

Month 3
Content cluster launch

Published 4 long-form blog posts targeting informational keywords around their practice areas. Built internal links from these posts to the relevant service pages. Set up Google Business Profile properly for local SEO.

Month 4
Rankings begin moving

First significant ranking movements. 11 keywords moved onto page 1. Organic traffic crossed 1,800 monthly visitors. Published 4 more blog posts. Added 3 client testimonials with structured markup to the homepage.

Month 5
3,500+ visitors, 3 new client enquiries per week

Traffic hit 3,500+ and kept climbing. 28 keywords on page 1. The firm started receiving 3 qualified online enquiries per week from organic search — versus near zero before I started. SEO retainer renewed for the next 6 months.

## The Three Things That Drove Most of the Growth - **The technical rebuild.** A PageSpeed score of 34 was actively suppressing every page on the site. Google doesn't rank pages it can't crawl and render quickly. Fixing this was the foundation for everything else. - **Matching content to search intent.** Their service pages were written for existing clients who already knew the firm — not for people searching "commercial property lawyer Mumbai" who had never heard of them. Rewriting for the searcher, not the client, was the biggest content shift. - **Consistency.** Eight blog posts over three months isn't a lot, but it was eight more than they'd published in the previous three years. Google rewards sites that publish regularly. The consistency signal alone accelerated indexing and crawling of the whole site.
**The honest takeaway:** This wasn't magic. It was a broken technical foundation repaired, content aligned to what people actually search, and a consistent publishing schedule maintained. If your site is in a similar situation, the same approach works. [I're happy to talk through what it would look like for your business.](contact.html)
